questions.stem: A bag contains red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 0.3, P(blue) = 0.45. These colours are mutually exclusive. What is P(green)?
questions.explanation: Since the events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (they cover all outcomes), P(red) + P(blue) + P(green) = 1. So P(green) = 1 − 0.3 − 0.45 = 0.25.

questions.stem: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a queen or a jack?
questions.explanation: Drawing a queen and drawing a jack are mutually exclusive (a card cannot be both). P(queen or jack) = P(queen) + P(jack) = 4/52 + 4/52 = 8/52 = 2/13. Option (a) multiplies instead of adding (a very common error).

questions.stem: For a biased dice: P(1) = 0.1, P(2) = 0.15, P(3) = 0.2, P(4) = 0.2, P(5) = 0.15, P(6) = 0.2. What is P(even number)?
questions.explanation: P(even) = P(2) + P(4) + P(6) = 0.15 + 0.20 + 0.20 = 0.55. For a biased dice, P(even) is not necessarily 0.5 as it would be for a fair dice.

questions.stem: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur at the same time, so P(A and B) = 0. Option (a) is P(A or B). Option (b) incorrectly multiplies as if the events were independent.

questions.stem: A spinner has sections labelled 1 to 10. P(prime) = 0.4 and P(square number) = 0.2. Emily says P(prime or square) = 0.6. Is Emily correct?

options.text: Yes, because you add the probabilities
No, because prime and square are not mutually exclusive (1 is both)
Yes, because these events are mutually exclusive

questions.explanation: The primes from 1-10 are {2,3,5,7} and the square numbers are {1,4,9}. These sets have no overlap (1 is NOT prime), so the events are mutually exclusive. P(prime or square) = 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6. Emily is correct.
